newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia editor's murder tied to "narco-terrorism".
newsitem.headline: Colombia editor's murder tied to "narco-terrorism".

text.p: A top newspaperman was shot and killed in southwest Colombia in a crime the nation's top general on Friday blamed on "narco-terrorism".

Gen. Harold Bedoya, the armed forces chief and a cousin of the victim, said the murder of Gerardo Bedoya Borrero was "one more crime of the many committed by narco-terrorism" and vowed to bring the killers to justice.

Police said Gerardo Bedoya, the 55-year-old director of the editorial section of Cali's respected El Pais newspaper, was shot six times by an unidentified gunman as he left an apartment building in the city centre on Thursday evening.
The killing was the second involving a Colombian journalist this week.

Gerardo Bedoya had campaigned from El Pais' editorial pages against the corrosive influence of drug trafficking on virtually all walks of life in Colombia and Gen. Bedoya said he had no doubt who killed his first cousin.
"It's one more crime of the many committed by narco-terrorism in Colombia, that's the reality," he told reporters.
"All Colombians have to become aware of the need to make these delinquents pay for their crimes," he said.
He did not elaborate, but as armed forces chief and acting defence minister Bedoya has control over the National Police and access to their evidence.

Police, who announced earlier that they were offering a $50,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of Bedoya's assassin, had said earlier that there were no immediate leads as to who was responible for the killing.

A former congressman and Colombian representative before the European Union, Gerardo Bedoya took up his post at El Pais five years ago. He had also worked as managing editor of the Bogota-based opposition daily El Nuevo Siglo.
Bedoya was a fierce critic of President Ernesto Samper, whose 1994 election campaign is alleged to have received millions of dollars in drug money.
But in a brief letter to the publisher of El Pais, Samper noted that he and Bedoya were fellow students at Bogota's Jesuit-run Javeriana University and said he deeply regretted his killing.
Bedoya should be remembered for his "sharp, polemical and brillant temperment" and the "convincing manner throughout his life with which he defended his ideas and principles," Samper said.
More than 100 journalists have been killed in Colombia since 1975, according to the Interamerican Press Association.

The killing of Bedoya came just one day after Freddy Elles, a photographer who worked for Bogota's El Espectador newspaper and El Heraldo de Barranquilla, was found handcuffed and stabbed to death in Caribbean port city of Cartagena.
